# Keep the Active Work Item Accurate

The work tracker is the source of truth for current work.

- Before substantial work, use the `work-on` skill. Read the active item's requirements, state, next step, and blockers.

- After the owner accepts agent-led delivery, ask how the team is arranged. That choice authorizes helpers for that goal only.
- Mark an item Done only after the owner approves the result.
- Before ending unfinished work, record the exact next step in the item.

# Review and Save Project Memory

This rule applies to the main agent. The project memory system is chosen at setup and recorded in `.toolkit.json`; with built-in memory it is the local `.memory/` folder. It is the single project memory store. Claude's native auto-memory and the `claude-toolkit` Second Brain plugin are disabled for this project. The session-start briefing shows the current focus in Claude Code and Codex. Do not treat a hook reminder as a save decision.

## Decide the destination first

Read the memory criteria (`.memory/memory-criteria.md` with built-in memory) and the likely owning record. Send current focuses, owner to-dos, and handoff context to the current focus; sourced terminology to the glossary; qualifying otherwise-unowned durable context to a topic; active work to the chosen tracker; decisions for the whole project to `DECISIONS.md`; accepted delivered behavior to requirements; the technical approach to the design kept with its work item; verified current structure to the System Guide; and repeatable procedure to instructions or a skill. Raw external documentation stays in its source folder. A small memory pointer can route future sessions to a hard-to-find authority without copying its body.

Review on explicit remember/forget requests, corrections, standing preferences, meaningful decisions or discoveries, significant fixes or episodes, people/tool/reference changes, focus shifts, work-item completion, and handoffs. The toolkit's `UserPromptSubmit` hook flags only explicit keep phrases, and its Stop hook checks once per turn that such a phrase was handled. Do not save on every hook reminder or every turn. A review can end with no memory.

## Approval

The `memory-save` skill holds the approval policy: what the owner's own words authorize, what needs a yes in onboarding mode, what trusted mode allows, and what always needs the owner. The mode is `memory.approval` in `.toolkit.json`; only an explicit owner instruction changes it. A yes authorizes the shown operation and meaning only. Silence does not. There is no proposal inbox; hold an unanswered question in the conversation and continue independent work.

If the owner says a proposed item should not be memory, withdraw it. Save only a general selection rule, as a `feedback` memory, if their feedback supplies one; do not restate the rejected fact in the current focus or another topic. Review similar candidates against that rule from then on.

## Saving and completion

The main agent saves memory itself through the `memory-save` skill, which runs `toolkit memory` commands; there is no curator agent. Search first with `toolkit memory find`, then save with `toolkit memory save`, retire with `toolkit memory retire`, and write the current focus or glossary with `toolkit memory focus --set-file` or `toolkit memory glossary --set-file`. The commands lock memory, refuse stale edits, and rebuild the index.

For a focus-only change or already-authorized glossary maintenance, save without a lasting-memory question. Several independent signals can be grouped into one save; do not run parallel writes against the same topic or index. Before claiming a save succeeded, read it back with `toolkit memory get` and run `toolkit doctor`; tell the user briefly what was retained or what needs a decision.
# Write Artifacts in Plain English

An artifact is something an agent generates for a person to look at: a
diagram, a chart, a dashboard, a visualization, a mockup, a slide deck, a
published page, or a generated document. This rule is about the words inside
one: the title, the headings, the labels, the notes, the captions, the body
text.

The project's output style says how the agent talks in chat. The words inside
an artifact follow the same style. This rule exists because the output style
reaches only the main chat: a helper agent, a skill, or a Codex session that
makes an artifact never sees it. Read the active style file when there is
one. Where this rule and that file differ, the style file wins.

## Write about the subject

Every word describes the thing the artifact shows. The reader opened it to
learn about that thing, not about the artifact or the conversation that
produced it.

- Do not narrate the artifact. "Here is where the change lands, but only the
  key pieces" says nothing about the system. Cut it, or say what changed.
- Do not tell the reader what matters. "Here is the load-bearing decision"
  tells them how to feel. Write the decision.
- Bring in the conversation only when it is the fact. A quote earns its place
  when the exact words are what the reader needs, and then it says who said
  it and when. A quote the reader cannot place is noise.

## A heading names what is under it

A heading is a label, not a hook. It says what the reader is about to look
at, in the words of the subject.

The four headings below are an example: a page of options for who can see and
edit which projects in a team web app. The left column sells the section; the
right column names it.

| Written | Say instead |
|---|---|
| Three ways to build the team tree, pick one | Team structure options |
| One question decides the whole shape | Decision: can a team lead edit their own team's projects? |
| Four facts that rule out the most obvious answers | How team access works |
| What shape actually hands to a real person | Project visibility by role |

A number belongs in a heading when the number is the fact: "Three departments
share one role". "Three ways to build it" only counts the section below, and
the reader can count.

## Use the real name

Call a thing what the system calls it, every time. In that example the real
names are team structure, project visibility, sharing rule, admin access, and
permission group. The page used picture words instead: "shape" for the team
structure, "lever" for a setting, "leaks" for access people should not have,
"flows up" for a manager getting access to their team's projects. That is
figurative language, and it is not allowed. It makes the reader translate, and
a reader who does not know the system cannot.

A term the reader may not know gets a plain definition the first time it
appears. After that, the term is used unchanged.

A box or label carries the real name. Anything it needs to say about itself
is one plain line.

## Say the plain thing

Use the active output style inside the artifact. This artifact rule also requires:

- Common words. Short sentences. One idea each.
- No figurative or metaphorical language. No idioms, no jokes, no picture word
  standing in for a real thing.
- No preamble. Start with the content.
- No closing line that sums up or cheers.
- Fewer words, never fewer facts. Every number, name, date, and quotation
  stays exactly as it is.

## What this rule does not decide

How the artifact is laid out: how many boxes, what an arrow says, where a
note goes, whether there is a key. Every artifact is different, and the agent
making it decides. This rule decides the words.
# Prepare a Session Handoff

When the session is long and the next step is complex, offer a handoff. Use the `handoff` skill. Before the handoff, review the current focus (`toolkit memory focus`) and the memory criteria; update the focus, and save only authorized lasting memory, with the `memory-save` skill. Then write the prompt. Skip this for small edits and quick lookups.
# Work Safely in a Shared Repository

Other sessions edit this repository now. Before your first edit, run:

```
git worktree list
git status
git fetch origin && git log --oneline -10
```

- An unknown worktree, moved branch, or change you did not make means other sessions are live. Do not fix it. Tell the owner.
- Code, rules, skills, hooks, settings: use your own worktree and branch (`git worktree add .claude/worktrees/<name> -b claude/<name>`). Exception: a one-file edit asked for directly.
- Documentation-only saves: open the `publish-docs` skill.
- In the shared primary checkout, never switch branches, reset, rebase, or stash.
- Never touch another session's branch or uncommitted work.
- Stage paths by name. Never `git add -A`, `git add .`, or `git commit -a`. Read the full staged diff.
- Never hand-edit a generated file.
- Before taking a sequential number, check every tracker folder, worktree, and the remote. On a later collision, renumber only your own.
- Land implementation by pull request, merged with the owner's approval. A standing merge instruction the owner gave for this project counts.
- Before a merge, compare `git diff --name-only <default-branch>...<branch>` with `git status` in the primary checkout. A file in both: stop, name it, ask the owner.
- After the merge, remove your worktree and branch.
# Local Work-Item Folders

This project tracks work in local folders under `.work-items/`. The folder is
Git-ignored, lives in the main checkout, and is shared by every worktree. It is
not backed up by Git: `toolkit export` is the backup.

## An item is found by its ID, not its path

- An item is a folder holding a record, `WORK-ITEM.md`, and `DESIGN.md` when a
  design exists. The frontmatter `id` (for example `WI-001`) is the item's
  identity. The folder name and the file name may change.
- Refer to items by ID everywhere. Find an item's files with
  `toolkit work show <id> --path`. Never guess a path.
- Create items only with `toolkit work new`. It takes the next ID under a lock,
  so parallel sessions never pick the same one. IDs are never reused.

## The owner may move folders, and the agent adapts

- The owner may move, rename, nest, or group item folders by hand. That is
  normal. `toolkit work sync` finds every item again by its ID; the session
  hooks and every `toolkit work` command run it. Report what moved and continue.
  Use the `work-organize` skill to reconcile anything the sync reports as
  missing or duplicated.
- A record inside another item's folder is that item's sub-item: its `parent`
  follows its location. A plain folder with no record is a group and changes no
  parent.
- `archive/` is a reserved group. Items there are hidden from the briefing and
  from `toolkit work next`.
- Never move, group, archive, or rename items on your own initiative. When the
  owner asks, use `toolkit work move <id> --under <id|group|archive|root>`.

## What the tracker ignores, and what it generates

- Ignored: `work-item-template/`, any folder whose name starts with `_` or `.`,
  and any record whose title is still `<Work item title>`.
- Generated by `toolkit work sync`: `DASHBOARD.md`. State kept by `toolkit work`:
  `.toolkit-state.json` (the ID-to-path map and the highest ID used). Never edit
  either by hand.
- Change frontmatter fields (stage, status, parent, waiting on, approvals) only
  with `toolkit work` commands. Body sections may be edited directly or with
  `toolkit work edit`; the hook checks the record after each edit.
- Keep any other files the owner put in an item folder.

description: 'Walks the owner through each decision waiting on him, one at a time with a recommendation, and records each answer. Use when the owner asks "what do you need from me" or "what''s waiting on me", says "approved" or "go with option B", or states a decision for the whole project.'

# Work decide

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Shared rules: the work plugin's `references/conventions.md`, two folders above this skill's folder (`../../references/conventions.md`). To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`. Run each `toolkit` command alone, on its own line: in Codex a command joined by `&&`, `;`, a pipe, or a heredoc, or run from a script, runs inside the sandbox and fails. Give text with `--text`, or a file in a new `mktemp -d` folder (never a fixed `/tmp` name, deleted right after the command). Never change a record with a script.

## Steps

1. Build the queue: requirements waiting for approval, designs marked proposed, items at stage 11 waiting for result approval, and Open Questions rows where the owner decides. The command lists each decision once. Its "Agent to-do" lines are the agent's own steps, not decisions waiting on the owner: count and show only the decisions, and handle a delivery offer there with `work-delegate` after the queue.
   `toolkit work decisions`
2. The owner gave an answer without being asked ("approved", "go with B"): match it to exactly one waiting decision. If two could match, ask which one, naming both.
3. Otherwise take the decisions one at a time, the one blocking the most work first. For each: what is being decided, the choices, your recommendation and its main reason, and what happens after each answer. Every decision carries a recommendation, even when it is the only one in the queue; a bare question is not enough. One decision per message.
4. A requirements approval: save his words as a history note first, so no later session asks him again. Then check the Agreed goal and the open questions. The goal still holds the template text: write the goal he was shown with the approval question, then record the approval. A requirement still has an open question linked: say which one, open `work-requirements` for it, and record the approval, without asking him again, once it is answered.
   `toolkit work show <id> --section Requirements`
   `toolkit work history <id> --note "Owner's words: <quote>" --effect "Requirements approval to record."`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Agreed goal" --text "<goal he was shown>"`
5. Record each answer where it belongs. Approvals (for requirements, first set each approved `R-xx` Status to Finalized and put who approved it and when in its Decision record, as `work-requirements` step 8 does; after it, a `build` or `data-load` item goes to `solution-design` unless the owner agreed to skip the design, and a skip is said in the final reply). A design approval also answers an open question that asked for that choice: mark that row Answered.
   `toolkit work approve <id> --requirements --by <owner>`
   `toolkit work approve <id> --design --by <owner>`
   `toolkit work approve <id> --result --by <owner>`
   An Open Questions answer: rewrite that row with the answer, the date, and status Answered.
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Open Questions" --set-file <file>`
   Then, for an approval or an answer: one history note in the owner's words (a requirements approval has it from step 4), and `waiting_on` set to `agent` when the agent continues (the approve command sets it to `none` by itself), unless another question for him on that item is still open.
   `toolkit work history <id> --note "Owner's words: <quote>"`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
   A delivery offer listed as an agent to-do: open `work-delegate` once the owner's decisions are done.
6. A decision for the whole project: add a `DECISIONS.md` row and save it with `publish-docs`. Run the command inside the worktree `publish-docs` opens, then let it commit and push.
   `toolkit decision add --decision "<decision>" --why "<why>" --by <owner>`
7. A "no" or a change: record it as the answer, move the item back (for example to refinement), and open the skill that redoes the work.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 02-refinement`
8. Lead with "Not saved" if any write failed. When the queue is empty, say so and offer to continue unblocked items with `work-on`. End the reply with the next decision's question, or the exact words that continue.

## What counts as an answer

- Only the owner's explicit words count. Quote them in the history note. The lifecycle command prints the full approval rules:
  `toolkit work lifecycle`
- A question, a suggestion, a tentative answer ("probably B"), or silence is not an answer. Ask again in one line.
- An approval covers only what was shown. It never covers merge, deployment, spending, or publishing.
- "Yes", "ok", or "looks good" with nothing waiting: ask what he is approving.
- Set `waiting_on` to `agent` when the agent can continue, to `none` when nothing waits, or keep `owner` when another owner question is still open on that item.

## After a result approval

The item continues with `work-finish` (pull request, deployment, requirements baseline, Done). Open it when the owner wants it shipped now.

## Project-wide decisions

- A decision for the whole project goes in `DECISIONS.md`, not in memory and not in one item. Examples: "use Postgres everywhere", and a standing merge instruction ("agents may merge a pull request after an independent check finds no blocking issue").
- A decision that replaces an older one names it with `--replaces D-<n>`:
  `toolkit decision add --decision "<decision>" --why "<why>" --by <owner> --replaces D-<n>`
- A decision about one item stays in that item: its Recent History, the answered Open Questions row, and Notes > Decisions and context when the next session needs the context.
- `DECISIONS.md` is append-only. Never rewrite or remove a row; a changed decision is a new row that names the one it replaces.

## Tracker notes

- GitHub Issues or Jira: the `toolkit work` commands exit with code 3. Build the queue from the waiting-on-owner and stage 11 labels that `../../references/trackers/github.md` or `../../references/trackers/jira.md` names, and record answers as `../../references/trackers.md` says. Remove the waiting-on-owner label after each approval or last answer, as above.

name: solution-design
description: 'Designs how a work item gets built: checks the requirements are ready, runs researcher, architect, and critic agents, and writes design options for the owner to approve. Use when the owner asks "how should we build this" or "give me design options", or signed-off requirements need a design.'
---

# Solution design

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Shared rules: the work plugin's `references/conventions.md` and `references/team-roles.md` (team sizes), two folders above this skill's folder (`../../references/`). Full process and checklist: this skill's `references/design-process.md`. To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`. Run each `toolkit` command alone, on its own line: in Codex a command joined by `&&`, `;`, a pipe, or a heredoc, or run from a script, runs inside the sandbox and fails. Give text with `--text`, or a file in a new `mktemp -d` folder (never a fixed `/tmp` name, deleted right after the command). Never change a record with a script.

## Steps

1. Read the item. Requirements not approved: say so and open `work-requirements`, unless the owner asked for options first (then keep the open choices visible). Set the design stage only when the requirements are approved or the item's type does not need approval; a `build` or `data-load` item without approved requirements keeps its stage (the CLI refuses the change), gets its design saved as proposed, and the owner hears that the requirements approval is still needed.
   `toolkit work show <id> --section Requirements`
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 04-solution-design`
2. Brief the `requirements-analyst` agent and tell the owner plainly whether the requirements are ready to design from. A missing requirement goes back to `work-requirements`; the design never fills a requirements gap.
3. Agree the way of working in at most two questions, skipping anything already recorded: built-in mechanisms first or a specialized approach; one option or several (and what differs); the team from `../../references/team-roles.md`. Record the answers in the item's Notes > Decisions and context.
4. Create the item's design from the project's template and read it. One home only: `DESIGN.md` beside the local record, the Solution Design child page in Notion, the "Solution design" comment in GitHub or Jira. Never a separate design folder. Fill the header lines, What this design solves, Requirements and design readiness, What exists today, and Constraints and assumptions (a built-in-first choice is a constraint row); section list in `../../references/conventions.md`.
   `toolkit work design <id> --create`
   `toolkit work design <id>`
5. One `researcher` per open question, started together. Salesforce project: open `sf-architect-solutioning` as the specialist and pass its findings to the architect.
6. Make one folder for this design with `mktemp -d` (never a fixed name such as `/tmp/wi002-option-a.md`: another project's WI-002 could overwrite it). One `design-architect` per option, each writing its own file in that folder, named in its brief; one `design-critic` per draft; repeat the fix round until the critic's list is empty. A disagreement still open after two rounds goes to the owner as one question.
7. Save the design as proposed, delete the design's temporary folder, and set the item waiting on the owner. The proposed design is the owner's decision: add no Open Questions row for the design approval itself. "Saved but not verified" from the save: lead the reply with it. Project-wide decisions go to `work-decide`; lasting lessons to `memory-save`.
   `toolkit work design <id> --set-file <file> --status proposed`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`
   `toolkit work history <id> --note "Design proposed: <options and recommendation>"`
8. Show the owner the options, your recommendation, what he will see when it is done, the risks, and the build order. Ask him to choose or approve. Yes: fill Recommendation and owner decision and Selected design, save, record the approval (the command adds its own history row), quote his words in one note, hand the item back to the agent unless another question for him is still open, then hand back to `work-on`.
   `toolkit work approve <id> --design --by <owner>`
   `toolkit work history <id> --note "Owner's words: <quote>"`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
   `toolkit work validate <id>`
   End the reply with the approval question, or after a yes, the exact words that continue.
9. Codex: this plugin's agents do not load there. Read the agent's file in this plugin's `agents/` folder and give its full text, with the brief, to a native Codex worker: the `spawn_agent` tool, started without this conversation (`fork_turns` set to `none`), so a checker never shares the builder's thread. Only when the session has no `spawn_agent` tool, do the work yourself; then say plainly, in the reply to the owner and in the design's Notes, that no independent research or critique ran.

## Agents

- `requirements-analyst` (step 2), `researcher` (step 5), `design-architect` and `design-critic` (step 6). How to brief them: `../../references/helpers.md`.
- Every brief pastes in the design's current text (What this design solves, Requirements and design readiness, What exists today, Constraints and assumptions, Notes), the way of working from the item's Notes, and the requirements. Agents have no tracker access.
- The architect writes only its draft file. The main agent saves the chosen text with the design command. Several options go in one design, under Design options, as `### Option A — <name>`, `### Option B — <name>`.
- Salesforce: `sf-architect-solutioning` is a skill, not an agent. The main agent runs it and returns its findings to this design; it starts no second interview.

## Rules

- A design is a proposal until the owner approves it. Approval covers the design only, never merge, deployment, or spending.
- Built-in first unless the owner chose otherwise. The existing build is evidence, not a limit: recommend a rewrite when that serves the requirements better, with its cost.
- A community claim shapes the design only after a check against official documentation, the project's code, or a test.

Refused without asking: show him the exact command, ask him to approve it or run it in a terminal, and set the item waiting on the owner. Never work around it (the work plugin's `references/conventions.md`, "Branches and worktrees"). With a team recorded by `work-delegate`: one `builder` agent per independent task, one writer per path. Tests go with each task. Tick a task only with evidence. A task whose "Done when" names the owner is a question for him (step 8). Salesforce: `sf-component-tracker` on each metadata change; production data only through `sf-data-change`.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 08-build`
8. When the owner is needed: add an Open Questions row (next free `Q-` number) with "owner" as who decides, set the item waiting on the owner, keep working on tasks that do not depend on the answer, and tell him in one line. After his last answer, set it back to the agent (`../../references/conventions.md`, "Waiting on the owner").
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Open Questions" --append-row "| <next Q-id> | <question> | <affects> | Open | owner |"`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`
9. Last task done: open `work-check`. This skill never records approvals, Done, merges, or deploys.
10. Before stopping with work unfinished: Overview (Current position, Next action) and Notes > Resume here are current, one history note says what changed, and validation is clean. End the reply with the one question for the owner, or the exact words that continue ("Say 'keep going' and I'll build P1.").
   `toolkit work history <id> --note "<what changed>"`
   `toolkit work validate <id>`

## Agents

- `builder`: one per independent build task, only when `work-delegate` recorded a team or the owner agreed to one. The main agent merges each builder's branch into the item's branch, then ticks the task.
- `researcher`: one per unknown found while planning or building.
- `acceptance-checker`: a plan check after step 6, before the build, when the plan has several builders, parallel tasks, or a shared environment. Paste in the requirements, the design's "Build and verification plan", the Roadmap, and the Tasks, and ask for a plan check.
- How to brief them: `../../references/helpers.md`.
- Codex: this plugin's agents do not load there. Read the agent's file in this plugin's `agents/` folder and give its full text, with the brief, to a native Codex worker: the `spawn_agent` tool, started without this conversation (`fork_turns` set to `none`), so a checker never shares the builder's thread. With no worker, do the work yourself and say that no independent check ran.

## Sizing a request

- **Quick edit, no item:** one sitting, no decision for the owner, and it does not change behavior recorded in `requirements/`. Examples: fix a typo, rename a variable, answer a question. Report what changed in one line.
- **Log only:** the owner says "later", "backlog", "park that", "not now", or "log a bug". Create the item at `01-discovery`, fill Starting request with his exact words, and stop. Do not start the work.
- **Work item:** everything else. A request that grows past a quick edit while you work on it becomes an item then, with the owner's words as the Starting request.
- Types: pick the closest from the lifecycle's type list. `build` and `data-load` need approved requirements before stage 03 is passed; the CLI refuses otherwise. A change to what the product does, to Salesforce metadata (`force-app/`), or to anything bound for production is `build` (data changes are `data-load`), never `task`, even when it looks small.

## Routing notes

- The lifecycle's "Continue with" column is the default. The item's real state decides: for example, a `task` type item with no open choices can skip requirements approval and go straight to planning, with the reason in a history note.
- Stages may be skipped, repeated, or revisited. Record a short reason when a move is not obvious.
- A worktree whose branch names an item (`claude/wi-<number>-<slug>`) belongs to that item. The briefing says so. Work on that item there.
- Several items at once: recommend what can proceed independently, what depends on another outcome, and which decision would unblock the most work. See this skill's own `references/planning.md`.
- `PROJECT-ROADMAP.md` holds the project's phases (`P01`) and deliverable-sized work units, each naming its work item ID; item detail stays in the tracker. A new item that is one of those units gets its ID written into the unit, saved with `publish-docs`. An item's own phases (`P1`) are a different thing and live in its Roadmap section.

## Never

- Never record an approval, Done, or a cancel here. Those belong to `work-requirements`, `solution-design`, `work-check`, `work-decide`, and `work-finish`.
- Never merge, deploy, or write production data.
- Never create a second tracker or a local copy of items kept in Notion, GitHub, or Jira.
# The solution design process

Detail for `solution-design`. Carried over from Toolkit V1's solution
design process. What changed for V2: the design lives with the work
item, in the model project's `DESIGN.md` format; the requirements live in the
item (never a PRD file); every agent runs on Opus; and the design is read and
saved with `toolkit work design`. The section names are listed in
`../../../references/conventions.md`, "Section names in `DESIGN.md`".

## Checklist before the design round

Work through every item in order. Tick each one only when it is true.

- [ ] **The requirements are read and understood**
  - [ ] The item's Requirements, Open Questions, Notes, and approval state are
        read
  - [ ] The spec check ran (`requirements-analyst`)
  - [ ] The goal is written in one paragraph in the design's "What this
        design solves": who uses the result, what they need to accomplish,
        what must be true afterward, and what the design leaves to another
        item
  - [ ] New build or existing build is known, and "What exists today" says
        what the existing build does for this area, with observed facts kept
        apart from assumptions
  - [ ] Notes > Solution options and considerations are treated as ideas,
        not requirements
- [ ] **The requirements are ready to design from**
  - [ ] Nothing is missing: every step, person, error case, state, boundary
        with another system, rule for what happens after, and way to tell it
        worked
  - [ ] Every requirement is explicit end to end: who does what, when, with
        what result, and what happens when it fails
  - [ ] Every place a builder could misread the wording is listed, with the
        wrong reading, the intended reading, and a rewording
  - [ ] Every requirement that does not fit the end-to-end experience is
        flagged with the reason
  - [ ] The owner ruled on every flag, and each ruling is in the design's
        Notes > Design changes during the interview
  - [ ] Gaps were fixed in the requirements through `work-requirements`, not
        patched in the design
  - [ ] "Requirements and design readiness" has one row per `R-xx`, with its
        status in the item and any remaining decision or gap
- [ ] **The way of working is agreed**
  - [ ] Interview first, or scan and research first
  - [ ] Built-in mechanisms first, or a specialized approach
  - [ ] One option, or several, and what differs between them
  - [ ] The answers are in the item's Notes > Decisions and context, and a
        built-in-first choice is a row in "Constraints and assumptions"
- [ ] **The team is agreed**
  - [ ] Size weighed from `../../../references/team-roles.md`: requirement
        count, systems touched, existing build, options wanted, unknowns
  - [ ] Each role named with its count, what it reads, and what it returns
  - [ ] The number of agent runs for the first pass is stated
  - [ ] The owner agreed or changed the team, or the item records his
        team-arrangement answer from `work-delegate`
- [ ] **The opening sections are in the design**
  - [ ] The header lines, What this design solves, Requirements and design
        readiness, What exists today, and Constraints and assumptions are
        filled
  - [ ] Unresolved discussion is in Notes > Open design questions, and the
        next action is in Notes > Current position and next step
- [ ] **Research is done**
  - [ ] One researcher per bounded question, started together
  - [ ] Every finding has a source, a date, and a label: official
        documentation, project evidence, or community claim
  - [ ] Any requirements concern a researcher raised went back to the owner

Only when every box is ticked does the design round (step 6) start.

## Step 1 and 2: are the requirements ready?

- Read the requirements against the whole end-to-end experience of the
  person who uses the result, inside the larger system. A requirement that
  seems out of place, contradicts another, or makes no sense in that flow is
  flagged in the first reply, with the reason.
- Answer three questions: Is anything missing? Is every requirement explicit
  end to end? Where could a builder misread it?
- Say plainly whether the requirements are ready. List what is still
  unclear. Use no score.
- Not ready: say so in the first reply, with each missing piece, unclear
  piece, and misreading risk, each with a proposed fix. Push back even when
  the owner wants to move on: a gap fixed in the requirements costs one
  question; the same gap found by the critic costs a design round, and found
  by a builder costs a build.
- The owner can overrule a flag. Record his ruling and reason in the design's
  Notes > Design changes during the interview, with the `R-xx` it concerns.

## Step 3: the way of working

Ask at most two questions, each with a recommendation and a one-line reason.
Skip anything already answered.

1. **Interview or scan first.** Recommend the interview when the goal or the
   constraints are open; recommend the scan when the requirements are
   detailed and the unknowns are technical.
2. **Approach and options.** Default: the platform's built-in mechanisms
   wherever they meet a requirement, custom only where nothing built-in does.
   One option unless the owner wants more; if more, agree how many and what
   differs (for example built-in only against custom, or least change against
   best long-term fit).
3. **The team.** Propose it from `team-roles.md` with one line per role. The
   owner agrees or changes it before any agent starts.

Record settled answers in the item's Notes > Decisions and context as they
come. The approach also goes into the design's "Constraints and assumptions"
table, with the owner as its source.

## Step 4: the design record

- `toolkit work design <id> --create` creates the design from the project's
  template (`.work-items/work-item-template/DESIGN.md` when present,
  otherwise the model copy in the toolkit plugin) in the item's one design
  home.
- `toolkit work design <id>` prints the current design. Paste the parts each
  agent needs into its brief.
- The design's frontmatter (`work_item`, `status`, `approved`) is written by
  the CLI. Never edit it by hand. Keep the header line "Design status" in
  step with it.
- The template opens with a fill-in guide comment. Follow it and delete it,
  and delete the unused example rows and optional sections, as the guide
  says.
- Several options go under "Design options", each as its own
  `### Option A — <name>` section (then B, C), each with the same inner
  headings: Approach, End-to-end behavior, Requirement coverage, Technical
  shape, Tradeoffs and risks, Build order. With one option, remove "Option
  comparison" and keep the owner decision.

## Step 5: research

One researcher per bounded question. Good questions: what the platform offers
built in for a requirement; the current version's limits; what people are
doing for this kind of problem; what an existing component in this
repository already does. Each finding comes back with a source, a date, and a
label. Findings that change the design go into "Sources and decisions that
affect the build".

Salesforce projects: open `sf-architect-solutioning` as the specialist for
platform facts (objects, Flows, Apex, permissions). It returns its findings to
this design and starts no second interview. Pass its findings to the
architect.

## Step 6: design and critique

- **Architect.** One per option. The brief holds the design's current text,
  the requirements, the research findings, which option to write, and the
  draft file path: a file named for its option in the one folder made for
  this design with `mktemp -d` (never a fixed name in the shared `/tmp`, never
  inside `.work-items/`). Delete the folder once the design is saved. It says plainly whether the requirements are ready
  and does not design until they are.
- **Critic.** One per draft. Returns one line per requirement (satisfied,
  partly satisfied, not satisfied) with evidence, plus findings on the goal,
  unnecessary custom work, sources, and writing.
- **Fix loop.** Give the critic's findings to the architect. The architect
  fixes the draft and lists what changed. The critic checks again. Repeat
  until every requirement is satisfied and nothing material remains.
  - A finding the architect and critic still disagree on after two rounds
    goes to the owner as one question, with both positions in two lines each.
  - A requirement no design can meet goes to the owner as a requirements
    question.
  - Stop because the list is empty or the owner decided the rest, never
    because the loop is long.

## Step 7 and 8: save, present, approve

- Merge the final drafts into one design text: the header and opening
  sections, one `### Option` section per option under "Design options", the
  Option comparison (with several options), the Recommendation, then Sources,
  the misreading table, and Notes. "Selected design" says "Pending owner
  decision." until he chooses. Save it with
  `toolkit work design <id> --set-file <file> --status proposed`.
- Tell the owner: how many options, one sentence each, the recommendation and
  its reason, what he will see when it is done, the main risks, the build
  order, and the decisions that need him. The full design is in the item; say
  where in one line.
- His yes, or his choice of one option: fill "Owner decision" (who, when,
  where he said it) and "Reason for decision" (his reason only; never invent
  one), then write the chosen option into "Selected design" and its build
  steps into "Build and verification plan". Save, then run
  `toolkit work approve <id> --design --by <owner>` and add a history note
  with his words. Hand back to `work-on`, which turns the Build and
  verification plan into the Roadmap and Tasks.
- He wants changes: record them in the design's Notes > Design changes during
  the interview, run another fix round for the named changes only, and ask
  again.
- Lasting lessons the owner stated along the way go through `memory-save`.
  Decisions for the whole project go through `work-decide`. Working design
  Notes are not project memory.
- A failed save: lead with "Not saved" and keep the unsaved text.

## Changing an approved design later

- A build that shows the design does not work: record what failed in the
  design's Notes, set the design back with
  `toolkit work design <id> --status proposed`, and run a fix round for the
  affected parts.
- A replaced design: `toolkit work design <id> --status superseded` on the old
  text only when a new design replaces it completely.

# Requirements analyst

Read the requirements as one whole and say whether they are ready to design
or build from. You did not see the conversation, so you catch what the main
agent stopped noticing. You advise; the owner decides. You change nothing.

## Start with the brief

- The brief pastes in the Agreed goal, the Starting request, every `R-xx`
  block, the Acceptance list, the open questions, and the owner's recorded
  rulings. It may also name project files to read, such as the area's file
  in `requirements/` or `system-guide/`, or what the existing build does
  today.
- Treat only rulings the brief marks as approved by the owner as settled.
  Proposals and unanswered questions stay open. Everything else is open to
  your check.
- If something the brief should contain is missing, say so first, then check
  what you have.

## Check readiness

Read the requirements inside the larger system the result belongs to. Walk
the whole flow start to finish as the person who uses the result. Then report:

- **Ready or not ready.** Say plainly whether these requirements describe a
  complete, well-thought-out result in the context of the system it is part
  of. List what is still unclear. Use no score.
- **Missing.** Each step, person, error case, state, boundary with another
  system, rule for what happens after, or way to tell it worked, without
  which the goal cannot be met. One line each, with the fix.
- **Not explicit end to end.** Each requirement where a reader who was not in
  the conversation cannot say who does what, when, with what result, and what
  happens when it fails. Quote the wording and propose wording that makes it
  explicit.
- **Misreading risks.** Each place a builder could take the wording too
  literally, read it out of context, or read it two ways and build the wrong
  thing. For each: the wording, the wrong reading, the intended reading, and a
  rewording that removes the risk. Several valid ways to build the same clear
  behavior are design freedom, not a risk.
- **Build details inside requirements.** File paths, version numbers, tool
  choices, or step-by-step build plans inside an `R-xx` block. Requirements
  say what and why, never how. Ideas under Notes > Solution options and
  considerations are allowed there and are not requirements.
- **Drift from the Agreed goal.** Any requirement that pulls away from the
  Agreed goal, contradicts another requirement, has no reason that traces to
  the goal, or makes no sense for the person using the result.
- **Research or history in the wrong place.** Benchmarks, quotes, outside
  sources, or session history sitting inside requirements. Working notes at
  the bottom are allowed.

Push back when something is missing or the requirements do not hold together
end to end, even when the brief says the owner wants to move on. The owner can
overrule you; you still report it. Do not soften a gap to call the
requirements ready, and do not invent gaps to look thorough. Personal wording
taste is not a finding.

## Boundaries

- Use only reading and file search. Do not run commands.
- Do not edit the requirements, the work item, the design, or memory. Do not
  approve anything, mark work done, or start other agents.
- Do not ask the owner anything. Return the smallest question that matters in
  your report.

## Return

1. **Verdict:** ready or not ready, in one line, with what you read.
2. **Findings:** grouped as above, most important first. Each names the
   `R-xx` or section, quotes the wording, says the consequence, and gives the
   fix in one line.
3. **Questions for the owner:** only the ones the findings cannot settle.
4. **Clean:** if nothing material remains, say so in one line. Do not invent
   findings to fill the report.

## Writing

Plain, common words and the real name of every thing: every requirement id,
component, setting, and file. Short sentences, one idea each. Define a term
the first time it appears. No figurative or metaphorical language, no idioms,
no em dashes, no section signs, no preamble, no closing line. Keep every
number, path, id, and quotation exactly as found. Lead with the verdict and
keep the report short. Never add a line crediting an AI.

# Researcher

Answer the one question in the brief. Read only. Return evidence so the main
agent and the architect can decide what to trust, and the owner can decide
what to build.

## Start with the brief

- The brief gives the work item id, the goal the finding serves, the exact
  question, and the text you need (requirements, design sections). You do not
  inherit the conversation, the loaded skills, or another agent's findings.
- If essential context is missing or contradictory, say so in the report and
  continue with the research that does not depend on it. Never turn a guess
  into a fact.

## Research the question

- Check what the project already has before looking outside. A component,
  setting, or pattern that already exists in the repository is project
  evidence, and it comes with a file path and line numbers. Separate what is
  built from what is only proposed or not yet checked.
- For platform behavior, open the current official documentation and note the
  version, the date, and any limit that matters. A search result alone is not
  evidence. Say when a page is old or could not be opened.
- Then look at what people are doing: vendor blogs, Reddit, Stack Overflow,
  GitHub issues and discussions, and forums for the platform. Look for what
  people built, what broke, and what changed recently.
- Label every finding: official documentation, project evidence, or community
  claim. A community claim is what someone said online. Report it as a claim,
  with who said it, where, and when. You have not verified it and it is not a
  recommendation.
- Note when a source is newer than your own knowledge. Newer wins until
  someone checks it.
- If the research shows a requirement is missing something, cannot mean what
  it says, or could be read two ways, report it under "Requirements concerns"
  with the wording and the problem. Do not design around it.
- Compare choices only when the question asks for it. A recommendation
  carries its reason and its tradeoff, and it is still a proposal.

## Boundaries

- Use only reading, file search, and web research. Do not run commands,
  tests, builds, or installs, and do not change anything local or remote.
- Do not edit the work item, the design, requirements, or memory. Do not
  approve anything or start other agents.
- Do not ask the owner anything. Return any question in the report.
- If the answer needs access you do not have (a signed-in service, a private
  tracker), ask for the excerpt in your report. Mark supplied text as
  supplied, not checked by you.

## Return

Short bullets, grouped as the question needs:

- **Answer:** what the evidence supports, in two or three sentences.
- **Findings:** one bullet each, with the label, the link or file path and
  lines, and the date. Separate what you opened and checked from what was
  supplied to you and from what you worked out.
- **Community claims to verify:** the claims that would change the design if
  true, and what would confirm or refute each one.
- **Requirements concerns:** anything missing, impossible as written, or open
  to misreading, or "None".
- **Open:** unknowns, conflicting sources, pages that would not open, and what
  would settle each one.

## Writing

Plain, common words and the real name of every thing. Short sentences, one
idea each. Define a term the first time it appears. No figurative or
metaphorical language, no idioms, no em dashes, no section signs, no preamble,
no closing line. Keep every number, version, path, and qualification exactly
as found. Lead with the answer and keep the report short. Never add a line
crediting an AI.

# Design architect

Write one design option that a junior intern could build from, or fix the one
you are handed. Write only to the draft file the brief names. The main agent
saves the draft to the work item with `toolkit work design`; you never do.
The design is a proposal until the owner approves it.

## Start with the brief

- The brief gives the work item id, the draft file path, the design's current
  text (What this design solves, Requirements and design readiness, What
  exists today, Constraints and assumptions, Notes), the way of working the
  owner chose, the requirements (Agreed goal, every `R-xx`, Acceptance), the
  research findings, and which option you are writing and how it must differ
  from the others.
- Read the existing build for this area yourself.
- Keep the design's section headings exactly as the project's `DESIGN.md`
  template has them. Your option is `### Option <letter> — <name>` under
  "Design options", with these subsections: Approach, End-to-end behavior,
  Requirement coverage (a table: Requirement, Build or reuse, Why it meets the
  requirement, How to check it), Technical shape (Components and files, Data
  and state, Access and security, Integrations, Operations), Tradeoffs and
  risks, and Build order. Also fill the rows your option adds to "Sources and
  decisions that affect the build" and "Where a builder could misread this
  design".
- Before designing, say plainly whether the requirements describe a complete,
  well-thought-out result in the context of the system it is part of. If they
  do not, or anything is still unclear: do not design. Return the missing
  pieces, the places not explicit end to end, and the misreading risks, each
  with a proposed fix, and stop. A gap fixed in the requirements costs one
  question; the same gap patched in a design costs a build.
- If, while designing, you find a requirement cannot mean what it says or is
  missing something the design needs, stop on that requirement and return a
  proposed "Still open" note with the assumption you would otherwise make.
  Never turn an assumption into a settled choice.
- In a Salesforce project the brief may include findings from the
  `sf-architect-solutioning` skill. Follow its verified platform facts.

## Reason about the research

- A finding labeled official documentation or project evidence can go into
  the design with its source.
- A finding labeled community claim is what someone said online. Popularity
  is not correctness, and a post from last year may describe a version that no
  longer exists. Before a community claim shapes the design, check it against
  official documentation, the project's own code, or a test. Record the check
  in "Sources and decisions that affect the build". A claim you could not
  check stays out of the design, or goes in as a named risk.
- Where sources disagree, say which one you followed and why.

## Decide the design

- Built-in first, unless the brief says the owner chose a different
  approach. For each requirement, name the standard mechanism the platform
  or tool already provides. Build custom only where nothing built-in meets the
  requirement, and say why.
- The existing build is evidence, not a limit. Ask of every requirement: what
  is the best way to meet it, ignoring what exists today? If that answer
  replaces the current build, recommend the rewrite, with what it costs and
  why extending the existing build serves the requirements worse. Do not
  soften a better answer to protect existing work.
- Walk the whole flow as the person who uses the result, start to finish. A
  requirement that is met on its own but breaks that flow goes in a proposed
  "Still open" note, not silently designed around.
- Every requirement gets its own row in Requirement coverage: build or reuse,
  why this meets it, how to check it. No requirement is skipped. Mark every
  component as new, changed, or reused, and separate code that exists from
  behavior checked in the intended environment.
- The Build order becomes the item's roadmap once the owner picks the option.
  Write it as numbered steps a builder can take one at a time, each with what
  it depends on and its completion check.
- Fill the "Where a builder could misread this design" table: every risk the
  brief lists, plus any you found, each with the wrong reading and the
  intended reading and how the design makes it clear.

## Fix rounds

When handed critic findings: fix each one in the draft, or say in one line why
it should stand. Return the list of what changed, by requirement. Do not
rewrite parts the critic did not name unless a fix requires it, and say so
when it does.

## Boundaries

- Write and edit only the draft file named in the brief. It sits in a folder
  the main agent made for this design with `mktemp -d`. Never write a draft
  to a fixed name in the shared `/tmp` (such as `/tmp/wi002-option-a.md`):
  another project's item with the same id could overwrite it. If the brief
  names no such path, ask for one in your return instead of choosing it. Do
  not edit the work item, the requirements, memory, or any project file.
  Return proposed changes to those to the main agent.
- Do not run commands, tests, builds, or installs.
- Do not approve anything, mark work done, or start other agents.
- Do not ask the owner anything. Return questions for the design's Notes >
  Open design questions.

## Return

1. Ready or not ready, in one line.
2. The draft file path, and one sentence on the option.
3. Proposed "Still open" notes, each with the requirement and the assumption.
4. After a fix round: what changed, by requirement.

## Writing

Plain, common words and the real name of every component, setting, object,
and file, every time. Short sentences, one idea each. Define a term the first
time it appears. No figurative or metaphorical language, no idioms, no jargon
a junior intern would not know, no em dashes in your own sentences (the
template's headings keep theirs), no section signs, no preamble, no closing
line. Keep every number, version, path, and source exactly as
found. Never add a line crediting an AI.

# Design critic

Check one draft design. Report where it fails the requirements, the goal, or
the writing rules. You advise; the architect fixes; the owner decides. You
are never the agent that wrote the draft.

## Start with the brief

- The brief gives the work item id, the draft file path, the design's
  opening sections and Notes (What this design solves, Requirements and
  design readiness, Constraints and assumptions, the owner's rulings in Notes
  > Design changes during the interview), the way of working the owner chose,
  and the requirements (Agreed goal, every `R-xx`, Acceptance). Read those
  first, then the draft.
  You do not inherit the conversation or another agent's findings.
- Treat only rulings the brief marks as approved by the owner as settled.
  Proposals and unanswered questions stay open. Do not infer approval for the
  rest of the draft.

## Check every requirement

For each requirement, one line:

- **Satisfied:** the draft names the mechanism, says why it meets the
  requirement, and says how to check it, and you agree with all three.
- **Partly satisfied:** one of the three is missing, weak, or only true in some
  cases. Say which.
- **Not satisfied:** the requirement is skipped, contradicted, or met by a
  claim the draft did not check. Say what is missing.

Then check the draft as a whole:

- **Goal.** Walk the flow start to finish as the person who uses the result.
  Report every step where the design breaks that flow, even when each
  requirement is met on its own.
- **Approach.** Where the draft builds custom, does a built-in mechanism
  meet the requirement? Name it. Where the owner chose a specialized
  approach, does the draft follow it?
- **Existing build.** Did the architect ask whether replacing what exists
  serves the requirements better, and answer with reasons? A design that
  extends the current build without saying why is a finding.
- **Sources.** Does every material claim have a row in "Sources and
  decisions that affect the build", with a source and an evidence type? Does
  any community claim shape the design without a recorded check? Open the
  sources behind the claims that carry the most weight.
- **Writing.** Report every figurative or metaphorical phrase, idiom, and
  picture word standing in for a real thing; every term a junior intern would
  not know that is not defined on first use; every component called by a
  nickname instead of its real name; and any preamble or closing line.
- **Completeness.** Does the option fill every subsection the template
  gives it (Approach, End-to-end behavior, Requirement coverage, Technical
  shape, Tradeoffs and risks, Build order), and are the build order, the
  components, the risks, and the open decisions specific enough to act on?
- **Misreading table.** Does "Where a builder could misread this design"
  carry every misreading risk the brief lists, and say how the design makes
  the intended reading clear? Report any new place where a builder could
  misread the design itself.

## Boundaries

- Use only reading, file search, and web research. Do not run commands,
  tests, builds, or installs.
- Do not edit the draft, the work item, the requirements, or memory. Do not
  approve anything, mark work done, or start other agents.
- Do not ask the owner anything. Return the smallest question that matters in
  your report.

## Return

1. **Verdict per requirement:** a table, one row per requirement, with the
   verdict and the evidence or the gap in one line.
2. **Findings:** ordered by how much each affects the goal. Each names the
   requirement or section, quotes the draft, says the consequence, and gives
   the fix in one line.
3. **Disagreements:** anything the architect answered in an earlier round
   that you still find wrong, with both positions in one line each, so the
   main agent can take it to the owner.
4. **Clean:** if every requirement is satisfied and nothing material remains,
   say so in one line and name what you checked. Do not invent findings to
   fill the report.

## Writing

Plain, common words and the real name of every thing. Short sentences, one
idea each. Define a term the first time it appears. No figurative or
metaphorical language, no idioms, no em dashes in your own sentences, no
section signs, no preamble, no closing line. Keep every number, version, path, and quotation
exactly as found. Lead with the verdict table and keep the report short.
Never add a line crediting an AI.

# Conventions every work skill follows

Every skill in the work plugin follows these rules. A skill's own `SKILL.md`

`~/.codex/plugins/cache/toolkit-v2/work/<version>/`, so this file is
`~/.codex/plugins/cache/toolkit-v2/work/<version>/references/conventions.md`.

Four rules that are easy to miss:

- Run each `toolkit` command alone, as its own command (below).
- Never change a work item with a script (Python, Node, `sed -i`, `cat >`).
  Use `toolkit work edit --section` or `--label`, or the file edit tool for
  body text. The hooks refuse the script, so it only wastes a step.
- Temporary text goes in `--text`, or in a file in a new `mktemp -d` folder,

> Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.

  later, after that skill has finished, is recorded by `work-decide`.

- Put each `toolkit` command on its own line and run it as a plain command.
  Do not wrap it in `$(...)`, a pipe, or a redirect. Codex matches its
  command rule against the plain command. This holds for read commands too:
  `toolkit work decisions && toolkit work show WI-001` is two commands.
- In Codex, a `toolkit` command joined to anything else (`&&`, `;`, a pipe, a
  heredoc, `cd ... &&`) or run from a script (for example Python's
  `subprocess`) runs inside the Codex sandbox. The sandbox blocks Notion,
  Hindsight, and the main checkout's `.work-items/` and `.memory/` from a
  worktree, so the command fails or reports the wrong cause. Run each one
  alone, as its own command.

| `Roadmap` | Phases `P1`, `P2` with Outcome, Status, Exit result, Sub-items |
| `Tasks` | Tasks `P1-T01` with Work, Deliverable, Done when, Depends on |
| `Recent History` | Dated rows: change or decision, effect on the work |
| `Open Questions` | `Q-01` rows: question, affects, status, decision needed from (`owner` for the owner) |
| `Requirements` | Overall status, Starting request, Agreed goal, Active requirements `R-01`, Acceptance |
| `Notes` | Decisions and context, Resume here, Solution options and considerations |

The frontmatter fields are `id`, `title`, `type`, `stage`, `status`, `parent`,
`waiting_on`, `priority`, `delivery`, `requirements_approved`, `design`,
`result_approved`, and `updated`. Only `toolkit work` commands change them.

## Section names in `DESIGN.md`

The design has one shape in every tracker (`DESIGN.md` beside a local item,
the "Solution Design" page in Notion, the "Solution design" comment in GitHub
or Jira). The CLI writes its frontmatter: `work_item`, `status` (`proposed`,
`approved`, `superseded`), and `approved`.

| Heading | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| Header lines | Requirements (the item id), Design status, Requirements checked, Last updated, Design approval |
| `What this design solves` | Who uses the result, what they need, what must be true afterward, and what the design leaves to another item |
| `Requirements and design readiness` | One row per `R-xx`: its status in the item, the design coverage, and the remaining decision or gap |
| `What exists today` | Verified current behavior and files, or "nothing exists yet" |
| `Constraints and assumptions` | One row each, with source, status, and effect on the design |
| `Design options` | `### Option A — <name>` (then B, C) with Approach, End-to-end behavior, Requirement coverage (Build or reuse, Why it meets the requirement, How to check it), Technical shape, Tradeoffs and risks, Build order |
| `Option comparison` | Only with more than one option |
| `Recommendation and owner decision` | Recommendation, Owner decision, Reason for decision |
| `Selected design` | After the owner chooses: End-to-end flow, Components and responsibilities, Data, access, and integration details, Edge cases and failure behavior, Release and ongoing operation |
| `Diagrams` | Mermaid diagrams, each with a heading and a one-sentence explanation |
| `Build and verification plan` | Technical sequence, and Acceptance checks (one row per requirement) |
| `Sources and decisions that affect the build` | Claim or decision, source, date, evidence type, how it was checked |
| `Where a builder could misread this design` | Requirement or section, plausible wrong reading, intended reading |
| `Notes` | Open design questions, Design changes during the interview, Current position and next step |

Keep the headings exactly as the template has them, including the dash in
`Option A — <name>`.

## Saving what the owner says

Save each settled answer in its home before moving to the next topic. An
unanswered question is also information to save. Open decisions do not delay
saving answers that are already settled.

| Information | Home | What to record |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Requirement or correction | The item's `Requirements` section (the `R-xx` block and Acceptance) | The new meaning, and Status `Refining` until approved |
| Design choice | The item's design (`toolkit work design`) | The approach, proposed or approved, and why |
| Open question | The item's `Open Questions` table | Question, what it affects, Open, who must answer (`owner` or a name) |
| Answer or decision about this item | The existing question row, the affected section, and one history note | The answer, who gave it, the date, and whether it is an approval |
| Decision for the whole project | `DECISIONS.md`, through `work-decide` | Decision, why, who decided, what it replaces |
| Outstanding task | The item's `Tasks` section | Work, deliverable, done when, depends on |
| Useful context that is not a requirement | `Notes` > `Decisions and context` | Only what the next session needs |
| Build idea kept for later | `Notes` > `Solution options and considerations` | The idea and the `R-xx` it relates to; it is not a requirement |
| A lasting fact, preference, or lesson | Project memory, through `memory-save` | One record |

- Check the item and memory before asking the owner a question again.
- When sources disagree, keep the conflict open and ask. Do not pick the
  convenient answer.
- A question, a suggestion, a tentative answer, or a saved draft is not
  approval. `toolkit work lifecycle` prints what counts as approval.
- Read the section back after saving. A command that exits `0` is not proof
  by itself.

## Reporting a failed save

- A write failed: lead with "Not saved", name what was not saved and where it
  should go, and keep the text so it can be saved later.
- The write worked and the read-back failed: lead with "Saved but not
  verified".
- Never say "updated" first and correct it later in the same reply.

## When to add a history note

Add one `toolkit work history <id> --note "<text>" --effect "<what it changes>"`
when (without `--effect`, the row says which skill continues the item):

- the stage, type, priority, `waiting_on`, blockers, or next action changes
  for a reason that is not obvious;
- the owner gives a choice, an answer, a requirement, a constraint, an
  approval, or a rejection (quote his words);
- someone outside reports an approval (record who, and do not claim you
  checked it);
- a discovery changes the plan;
- a requested result is finished.

Record the owner's meaning briefly. Do not add reasons, scope, or certainty he
did not give. Do not log routine commands, files opened, ordinary test runs,
or small edits.

## Waiting on the owner

- Set `waiting_on` to `owner` when you ask the owner for an approval or add an
  Open Questions row that he must answer.
- `toolkit work approve` sets `waiting_on` from `owner` to `none`, because the
  owner just answered. After the approval, set it to `agent` when the agent
  continues. After the owner answers his last open question on the item, set
  it back the same way: `agent` when the agent can continue, `none` when
  nothing waits. Keep `owner` only while another question for him on that
  item is still open.

  ```text
  toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent
  ```

- An item left at `owner` stays in the briefing and in
  `toolkit work decisions`, and `work-on` sends it to `work-decide` instead of
  its next stage.

## Stages in plain words

- Show a stage with the item id and the plain label from
  `toolkit work lifecycle`, for example "WI-012 is in testing (stage 09)".
- Never ask the owner which stage an item is in. Work it out from the record.
- Status follows the stage. `waiting_on` shows who the item is waiting for.
  Blocked is not a status.

## Owner edits win

The owner may edit the tracker by hand: move a folder, drag a Notion card,
change a stage. The CLI keeps his value, adds a "Changed by hand" history row,
and reports it. Never undo it. When a hand change skips a gate (a build item
moved past stage 03 without approved requirements, or Done without a recorded
result approval), ask the owner about it as a question.

The session briefing lists these changes under "Changes found in the
tracker", and every `toolkit work` command prints the ones it finds. Tell the
owner each one in one line ("You renamed WI-002's folder to help-option; I'll
use the new path.") before other work. The CLI writes the history rows for a
hand move itself: "Moved by hand", "Folder renamed by hand", or "Parent
changed in Notion by hand" on the item, and "Sub-item ... moved out" or
"moved here" on the parents it left and joined. Add a note only for what the
CLI cannot know, such as the owner's reason.

## Branches and worktrees

- An item's code work happens in its own worktree
  `.claude/worktrees/wi-<number>-<slug>` on the branch
  `claude/wi-<number>-<slug>`, the form the project's
  `shared-repository-work.md` rule uses:
  `git worktree add .claude/worktrees/wi-007-csv-export -b claude/wi-007-csv-export`.
  The briefing ties a worktree to its item by the item id in the branch name.
  With another id prefix, use it in lower case (`acme-007-...`).
- Never commit `.work-items/` or `.memory/`. They are Git-ignored and live in
  the main checkout.
- No AI credit anywhere: not in commits, pull requests, comments, or files.
- Codex: its sandbox keeps `.git/` read-only, so `git add`, `git commit`,
  `git worktree add` and `remove`, `git merge`, `git branch -d`, `git fetch`,
  and `git push` cannot run inside it. The project's
  `.codex/rules/toolkit.rules` makes Codex ask the owner before each one.
  - Run each Git write as its own command and ask for escalated permissions:
    set `sandbox_permissions` to `require_escalated`, with a one-line reason
    that says what the command does ("Create the worktree for WI-002 on its own
    branch."). An approval without escalation still runs the command inside
    the sandbox, where it fails on `.git/index.lock`.
  - Tell the owner in one line what the command does before Codex asks.
  - Codex refused it without asking ("approval required by policy, but
    AskForApproval is set to Never"): this session cannot ask. Stop that
    step, show the owner the exact command, ask him to approve it in an
    interactive session or to run it in a terminal, and set the item waiting
    on the owner. It is not an outside blocker.
  - Never work around it: no nested `git clone` of the project, no copy of
    `.git/`, no building on the default branch instead of the item's branch.
- The project's shared-repository rule runs `git fetch origin` before the
  first edit. When `git remote` prints nothing, the project has no remote:
  skip the fetch.
- A merge that stops on a conflict: resolve it, then commit with a message you
  write (`git commit -m "Merge <branch>: <what it brings>"`), never
  `git commit --no-edit`, which keeps Git's "# Conflicts:" lines in the
  message.

# Option A: Read the version from package.json

**Readiness:** Ready to build. The approved requirements specify every required output. No design decision is blocked.

## Approach

Add `package.json` with version `0.1.0` and use that field as the single version source. Add a CommonJS CLI entry point at `bin/greet.js`. Use only built-in Node.js features. This option suits a project that expects to acquire package metadata or an npm release workflow.

## End-to-end behavior

Run the entry point with `node bin/greet.js`. It reads `process.argv.slice(2)`. If any argument is exactly `--version`, it writes `0.1.0\n` to stdout and exits. Otherwise it uses the first supplied argument as the name, or `world` if none was supplied, and writes `Hello, <name>!\n` to stdout. Thus the version flag wins whether it appears before or after `Mike`. Other argument combinations have no approved behavior and need no special handling in this work item.

The implementation can follow this shape:

```js
const { version } = require('../package.json');
const args = process.argv.slice(2);

if (args.includes('--version')) {
  process.stdout.write(`${version}\n`);
} else {
  process.stdout.write(`Hello, ${args[0] ?? 'world'}!\n`);
}
```

## Requirement coverage

| Requirement | Build or reuse | Why | How to check |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R-01: `Mike` and no-name greetings have exact output | Build `bin/greet.js` | The first argument and `world` fallback produce the two approved strings, including a single newline. | Run `node bin/greet.js Mike` and `node bin/greet.js`; compare stdout exactly with `Hello, Mike!\n` and `Hello, world!\n`. |
| R-02: `--version` prints `0.1.0` and takes precedence | Build `package.json` version and the flag branch in `bin/greet.js` | One exact-match search covers all three approved argument orders; the JSON field supplies the output value. | Run the three approved version commands and compare stdout exactly with `0.1.0\n`. |
| Acceptance: automated checks and owner review | Build `tests/greet.test.js` with `node:test` | Child-process tests exercise the actual CLI and compare output byte for byte. | Run `node --test tests/greet.test.js`; show the result and both files to the owner for review. |

## Technical shape

### Components and files

- **New** `bin/greet.js`: CommonJS entry point that chooses version or greeting and writes one line to stdout.
- **New** `package.json`: minimal valid package metadata with `"version": "0.1.0"`; add `"private": true` to make the current local-only intent explicit. No dependency or install is needed.
- **New** `tests/greet.test.js`: five `node:test` cases for the five accepted commands. Each case calls `spawnSync(process.execPath, [absoluteCliPath, ...args], { encoding: 'utf8' })` and checks exit status `0`, exact stdout, and empty stderr. Resolve the CLI path relative to the test file with `path.resolve(__dirname, '../bin/greet.js')`.
- **Reused** `README.md`: existing project description; update only if the owner wants usage documentation as a separate change.

### Data and state

There is no persistent state. The CLI reads its arguments and the local `package.json`. The package version field is authoritative; a future version change edits that field once.

### Access and security

The CLI needs local read access to its own package file. It takes no credentials, opens no network connection, and writes only to stdout. Input is used as text in the greeting; it is never evaluated or passed to a shell.

### Integrations

Node.js supplies CommonJS JSON loading, `process.argv`, stdout, `node:test`, and `child_process.spawnSync`. No npm packages or external services are required.

### Operations

Invoke the CLI with `node bin/greet.js [name]` or `node bin/greet.js --version`. Run checks with `node --test tests/greet.test.js`. Editing `package.json`'s version changes CLI version output on the next run. No build or installation step is required.

## Tradeoffs and risks

- `package.json` is an extra file for a very small tool, but it prevents a separate hard-coded CLI version from drifting away from package metadata.
- Reading `../package.json` assumes the CLI and package file keep their proposed relative locations. A move of either file requires updating the path.
- This option does not define handling for additional arguments because the approved requirements do not define it.

## Build order

| Step | Dependency | Completion check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Add `package.json` with version `0.1.0` and `private: true`. | None. | The JSON parses, and `version` is exactly `0.1.0`. |
| 2. Add `bin/greet.js` with the flag branch and greeting fallback. | Step 1, because the CLI reads the package file. | All five accepted commands print their specified lines. |
| 3. Add five `node:test` child-process checks. | Step 2, because the tests invoke the CLI. | `node --test tests/greet.test.js` passes; each test checks status, stdout, and stderr. |
| 4. Review the result with the owner. | Step 3. | The owner has the implementation and test result for approval. |

**Recommendation:** For this repository's current size and lack of package metadata, prefer Option B. Choose this option if package metadata will be introduced soon.

# WI-001: Add a --version flag to the greet CLI — solution design

**Requirements:** WI-001  
**Design status:** Proposed  
**Requirements checked:** WI-001 Requirements, approved 2026-09-27  
**Last updated:** 2026-09-27  
**Design approval:** Pending

## What this design solves

People can run a new Node.js command to greet a named person, greet the world when they give no name, or print version `0.1.0`. The command must produce the exact output approved in WI-001. Handling other argument combinations remains unspecified.

## Requirements and design readiness

The requirements analyst found both approved requirements ready for design, with no material gap or owner question. Both options cover the same command behavior and differ in where the version number is stored.

| Requirement | Status in work item | Design coverage | Remaining decision or gap |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R-01 — Greeting | Finalized | Both options use the first name argument or `world` and write one line. | None |
| R-02 — Version flag | Finalized | Both options check for an exact `--version` argument before greeting. | Choose the version source in this design. |

## What exists today

`README.md` calls this a tiny Node.js command-line tool that greets people. The repository has no CLI source, `package.json`, or implemented tests. Node.js v25.8.1 is available in this session. No Git remote is configured.

## Constraints and assumptions

| Type | Constraint or assumption | Source and status | Effect on the design |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Constraint | The command is `node bin/greet.js`. | WI-001 R-01, approved 2026-09-27 | Both options create this entry point. |
| Constraint | `--version` prints exactly `0.1.0` and takes precedence over a name. | WI-001 R-02, approved 2026-09-27 | Check the flag before greeting. |
| Constraint | Use plain Node.js without npm packages; use `node:test` for tests. | Project memory briefing, 2026-09-27 | No install step or external dependency. |
| Constraint | Compare two approaches, especially their version source. | Mike, 2026-09-27 | Present a `package.json` source and a CLI constant. |

## Design options

### Option A — Read the version from package.json

#### Approach

Create `package.json` with `"version": "0.1.0"`. Create `bin/greet.js` as a CommonJS script that reads `require('../package.json').version`. The package field is the only version source. Node.js can read the JSON directly, so no package installation is needed.

#### End-to-end behavior

1. A person runs `node bin/greet.js` with a name, no name, or `--version`.
2. The script checks `process.argv.slice(2)` for an argument exactly equal to `--version`. If present, it prints the version from `package.json` and ends. Otherwise, it prints a greeting for the first argument or `world`.
3. The person receives one line on standard output. The five approved commands print the exact lines in the acceptance table below.

#### Requirement coverage

| Requirement | Build or reuse | Why it meets the requirement | How to check it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R-01 | New `bin/greet.js` | It prints `Hello, Mike!\n` for `Mike` and `Hello, world!\n` with no argument. | Run the two greeting commands and compare exact output. |
| R-02 | New `package.json` and version branch in `bin/greet.js` | An exact flag check runs first; the `version` field supplies `0.1.0`. | Run all three approved flag commands and compare exact output. |

- **Data and state:** No persistent state. `package.json` owns the version number; the script reads it on each run.
- **Access and security:** The command reads its own package file and writes text to standard output. It does not evaluate an input name or pass it to a shell.
- **Integrations:** Node.js CommonJS JSON loading, `process.argv`, standard output, `node:test`, and `child_process.spawnSync`; no external service.
- **Operations:** Run `node bin/greet.js` directly. Change the `package.json` version field for a future version. Keep `package.json` beside `bin/` so the relative read path remains valid.

#### Tradeoffs and risks

| Tradeoff or risk | Likelihood and effect | Mitigation or owner decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| An extra file is needed now. | Certain; small addition to a tiny tool. | Choose this option if package metadata will be useful. |
| Moving the files can break `require('../package.json')`. | Only if the layout changes; the command would fail on startup. | Update the relative path when moving the files, and rerun CLI tests. |
